source: Wald (1945) Sequential tests of statistical hypotheses (Annals of Math. Statistics 16)
finding: Founding paper of the SPRT. After each observation compute the likelihood ratio of H1 to H0. Stop and accept H1 if it passes an upper bound, stop and accept H0 if it falls under a lower bound, otherwise take one more observation. Sample size is random, not fixed.
numbers: Wald's thresholds, as quoted by Stefan et al. 2022 (read): A=(1-beta)/alpha, B=beta/(1-alpha); true error rates are bounded by alpha'<=1/A and beta'<=B.
limits: Publisher page blocked, so the paper itself was not read. Details come from secondary texts that I did read (a02, a05). Two simple hypotheses only. Error bounds are approximate because the ratio can overshoot a bound.
agent_relevance: The core template for stop when the evidence suffices: two bounds, one running score, a pre-set error budget.

source: Wikipedia: Sequential probability ratio test
finding: SPRT accepts H1 when the cumulative log likelihood ratio S passes b, accepts H0 when it falls below a, else continues. Approximations a=log(beta/(1-alpha)), b=log((1-beta)/alpha), a<0<b. Exact for continuous paths, approximate in discrete steps because of overshoot. Neyman-Pearson (1933) motivated Wald's reformulation.
numbers: Example: defect rate tested at p1=0.01 vs p2=0.03 in quality control. MaxSPRT (Kulldorff 2011) adds a composite one-sided alternative. Spiegelhalter et al. used SPRT charts for surgeon outcome monitoring.
limits: Encyclopaedic page; no expected-sample-size figure on it.
agent_relevance: Gives the exact stop rule we could code: add a log-ratio per sample, compare to two constants set by alpha and beta.

source: Wikipedia: Sequential analysis
finding: History. Wald worked with Wolfowitz, Wallis and Friedman in Columbia's Statistical Research Group in WWII; the method was used in industrial quality control and was classified as restricted. Barnard led a parallel British group. Turing independently used a similar approach in Banburismus at Bletchley Park, secret until the early 1980s. Armitage brought it to medicine; Pocock gave Type-1 control for group designs.
numbers: Pocock boundary: looks must be pre-set and equally spaced. O'Brien-Fleming, Wang-Tsiatis, Haybittle-Peto are alternatives. Lan-DeMets alpha-spending removes the fixed-look restriction.
limits: Page gives no numeric inflation figures. Claims not checked against primary sources.
agent_relevance: Shows the idea is old and general: repeated looks need a rule that pays for the looks (alpha spending).

source: Wald and Wolfowitz (1948) Optimum character of the sequential probability ratio test
finding: Proved that among all tests (sequential or not) with error probabilities no larger than a given SPRT, the SPRT has the smallest expected sample size under both H0 and H1.
numbers: Operational statement from a search snippet (not the paper): fewest observations on average of all tests with the same power. One lecture page claims roughly 2-3 times saving in a Gaussian shift example (unverified).
limits: Optimal only at the two named parameter values. At other values the SPRT's expected sample size can be much larger than a fixed-sample test. Not read; publisher blocked.
agent_relevance: Justifies the SPRT as the cheapest stop rule for a two-way question, but warns that vote shares near the middle are the costly case.

source: Stefan, Schoenbrodt, Evans, Wagenmakers (2022) Efficiency in sequential testing: SPRT vs sequential Bayes factor test (Behav Res Methods)
finding: SPRT and the Sequential Bayes Factor test (SBFT) are two instances of one framework: both monitor a relative-evidence ratio and stop when it crosses a boundary. Their efficiency difference depends on how the alternative is specified, not on philosophy.
numbers: Cites that sequential designs consistently cut sample size by 50% or more against fixed-sample designs. Wald thresholds A=(1-beta)/alpha, B=beta/(1-alpha) can over-control error rates. Schnuerch and Erdfelder (2020) found the SPRT t-test more efficient than a Bayesian t-test with diffuse priors; Stefan et al. show that was an extreme case, and with informed priors the SBFT is no longer less efficient.
quote: Studies investigating the efficiency of sequential designs have consistently found reductions in sample sizes of 50% or more
limits: Psychology t-test setting, not LLM voting. Informed priors give efficiency but less robustness under misspecification.
agent_relevance: A prior on how strong the winner is changes how fast we stop. Wide priors are robust, narrow priors are fast but brittle.

source: Stefan et al. (2022), same paper: threshold optimisation and cost
finding: Wald's constant thresholds deviate most from optimal thresholds for large effects, where expected sample sizes are already small, so optimising thresholds yields small absolute savings.
numbers: Authors: even the least efficient sequential design is typically more efficient than the most efficient fixed-sample design.
limits: Savings matter most when each observation is costly. Simulation-based on t-tests.
agent_relevance: An extra LLM sample is costly, so even small savings count.

source: Johari, Pekelis, Walsh (2015/2019) Always valid inference: continuous monitoring of A/B tests
finding: Fixed-horizon p-values are invalid if users stop when they like. Defines always-valid p-values and confidence intervals via the mixture SPRT (mSPRT, Robbins 1970), which has power one. Deployed in a commercial A/B platform over hundreds of thousands of experiments.
numbers: Fig 1: an A/A test (both arms identical) where 1-p rises above the 95% line under continuous monitoring, a Type I error. Misspecifying the mixture variance by two orders of magnitude costs under 5% average power and under 10% run-length; missing by more can cost 20% power and 40% run-length (Section 5.6).
limits: Needs a mixing prior; run-length gains hold on average, not for each test.
agent_relevance: Our agent peeks after every sample. Repeated peeking at a fixed 95% threshold inflates false stops; use an mSPRT or similar.

source: Howard, Ramdas, McAuliffe, Sekhon (2021) Time-uniform, nonparametric, nonasymptotic confidence sequences (Ann. Stat.)
finding: Builds confidence sequences valid at all times simultaneously, via Ville's inequality on nonnegative supermartingales and conjugate mixtures or stitching. Width shrinks at rate O(sqrt(log log t / t)), matching the law of the iterated logarithm.
numbers: Traces roots to Ville (1939), Wald (1945), Darling and Robbins (1967, 1968), Robbins (1970). Sub-Gaussian conjugate-mixture boundaries are unimprovable without further assumptions (Section 3.6).
limits: Nonparametric bounds are wider than parametric SPRT bounds when the model is right.
agent_relevance: A distribution-free route to a stop rule for bounded vote data: no model of the LLM needed.

source: Ramdas, Grunwald, Vovk, Shafer (2023) Game-theoretic statistics and safe anytime-valid inference (Statistical Science)
finding: Evidence is a betting score (e-value) with expected value at most 1 under the null; the sequential version is an e-process. Tests built this way allow stopping or continuing for any reason without breaking error control. Roots in Ville (1939), Wald (1947), Robbins.
numbers: Motivating case: the power-posing study team ran subjects in chunks and checked the effect along the way. Barnard's 1947 review of Wald's book asked for stop-or-continue deliberation after each batch.
limits: Survey, no new experiments. The authors say these ideas were a small niche until about 2017.
agent_relevance: The modern, safest framing of stop when sure: a running wealth score that can be checked after every sample.

source: Grunwald, de Heide, Koolen (2023) Safe testing
finding: E-value tests are safe, meaning they keep Type-I error guarantees under optional continuation. Defines growth-rate optimality (GRO) as the analogue of power; GRO e-values take the form of Bayes factors with special priors.
numbers: No single headline number; theorems and examples (t-test, 2x2 tables).
limits: Theory paper; efficiency versus classical tests depends on the alternative.
agent_relevance: Bayes-factor-like running scores can be made valid under any stopping rule; useful for an S0 gate that checks evidence repeatedly.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-consistency improves chain of thought reasoning in language models (ICLR)
finding: Sample many reasoning paths, majority-vote the final answer. Gains over greedy CoT on PaLM-540B with 40 samples averaged over 10 runs. This fixed-budget vote is the baseline every LLM stopping paper tries to cut.
numbers: Gains: GSM8K +17.9%, SVAMP +11.0%, AQuA +12.2% absolute; 40 sampled outputs per question; unweighted majority vote did as well as probability-weighted aggregation (Table 1).
limits: Fixed n=40 for every question, easy or hard. Samples come from one model, so errors correlate (guardrail G4).
agent_relevance: The baseline. Our agent treats agreement as a hint, never as proof.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Let's sample step by step: Adaptive-Consistency (EMNLP 2023)
finding: Sequential stopping for voting. Draw samples one at a time; model answer counts with a Dirichlet (simplified to a Beta on the top two answers, prior Beta(1,1)); stop when the posterior probability that the leader stays on top exceeds a threshold. No fixed budget.
numbers: 17 datasets, 3 LLMs, max 40 samples (code: 50-100 per problem). Up to 7.9 times fewer samples, mean accuracy drop under 0.1%. Math 3.3x fewer (acc 73.2 to 73.1; samples 40 to 13.8); commonsense 2.9x (66.0 to 65.8; 40 to 15.8); symbolic 3.8x (72.8 to 72.8; 40 to 13.1); code 2.4x (35.2 to 35.6; 312.5 to 173.6). GPT-3.5-Turbo 4.4x (76.4 to 76.2); Vicuna-13B 1.9x (54.0 to 54.1); Code-davinci-002 3.4x (69.7 to 69.8). Example: 9 of the first 10 agree, so 30 samples are saved.
limits: Bayesian rule ignores repeated-look Type I error (ConSol critique). Weaker models save less (Vicuna 1.9x). Threshold must be tuned.
agent_relevance: Strong precedent for stop after enough agreement: 2-4 times fewer samples at about no accuracy loss, mostly on easy items.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Adaptive-Consistency: stopping criteria compared and the threshold curve
finding: Compared Beta, Dirichlet, Chinese Restaurant Process, entropy and plain stop-at-majority criteria. Beta is the default as it is nearly as good and cheaper. Sweeping the confidence threshold 0.5 to 1: accuracy climbs then plateaus, while average samples rise slowly then steeply.
numbers: Curve shown on GSM-8K; cost grows steeply as threshold approaches 1.
limits: Equal-cost comparison with fixed-k SC is in Section 5.2; exact crossing numbers not copied here.
agent_relevance: One dial (threshold) trades cost for accuracy; set it per task from our own held-out data.

source: Li et al. (2024) Escape sky-high cost: Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ICLR 2024)
finding: Split the sample budget L into windows of size w. Stop at the first window in which all w answers are identical (window entropy zero). Argued via a null-hypothesis test that a fully agreeing window means the top answer is likely the mode.
numbers: Sampling cut: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%, with comparable accuracy (window 5, MATH window 8, 10 runs averaged; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2). Matched-cost SC differs by under 1 point in most cells.
limits: Window size and L need tuning; the paper adds a control scheme using the first window. MATH is hardest to cut. GPT-4 Coin Flip at 100% so untested.
agent_relevance: Simplest code rule: five agreeing samples in a row means stop.

source: Wan et al. (2025) Reasoning Aware Self-Consistency (RASC)
finding: Scores each sample on answer consistency and reasoning-path quality, stops when a buffer of N high-quality samples agrees, then weights the vote. Beats AC and ESC on samples used.
numbers: Abstract: about 70% fewer samples at maintained accuracy; about 80% less inference time than SC. Ablation (averaged): answer-level only 10.86 gens at 55.5 acc, reasoning-level only 5.50 at 50.4, combined 8.20 at 55.8 (first column group).
limits: Feature extraction adds cost and uses an LLM scorer. Thresholds T and buffer N need tuning.
agent_relevance: Agreement plus a per-sample quality signal can stop earlier, but a scorer is a model judgement (guardrail G5).

source: Wang et al. (2025) Make every penny count: Difficulty-Adaptive Self-Consistency (DSC)
finding: Ranks question difficulty first, gives easy ones one sample, pre-allocates samples to hard ones. Also counts input-token cost that sequential stopping repeats on each re-sample.
numbers: GSM8K: CoT and 40-sample SC agree in 84.8% of cases for GPT-3.5-Turbo and 96.2% for GPT-4 (Fig 1). Cost cut vs SC: 65.29% on GPT-4 and 56.04% on GPT-3.5-Turbo; vs ASC/ESC 24.81% and 21.86%; six benchmarks.
limits: Needs a batch of questions for the difficulty ranking; the difficulty judge is an LLM call.
agent_relevance: Most questions need one sample. A cheap first-pass gate before sequential sampling beats a tighter stop rule.

source: Taubenfeld et al. (2025) Confidence improves self-consistency in LLMs (CISC)
finding: Weighted majority vote with the model's own confidence in each path. Reaches the right answer with fewer samples. The most calibrated confidence method was the least useful for CISC; within-question discrimination is what matters.
numbers: Nine models, four datasets: over 40% fewer reasoning paths on average; Gemma2-9B on MATH: 8 CISC samples beat 30-sample SC (73% cost cut, Fig 1).
limits: Not an early-stopping rule; it changes the vote. Self-confidence can be unreliable across questions.
agent_relevance: A weight could sit in the evidence sum, but our rules G2/G5 prefer code-based scores.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Stops single traces early when group confidence falls under a threshold set from a 16-trace warmup. Also an adaptive budget: stop adding traces once vote consensus passes a preset ratio.
numbers: AIME 2025, GPT-OSS-120B: DeepConf@512 99.9% vs 97.0% for majority at 512 and 91.8% pass@1 (offline). Online mode cuts generated tokens by up to 84.7% while maintaining or exceeding accuracy.
limits: Needs token logprobs and a warmup (N_init=16); open models only (Qwen3, GPT-OSS, DeepSeek-8B).
agent_relevance: A second stop signal at trace level, not only at answer level.

source: ConSol authors (2025) ConSol: Sequential Probability Ratio Testing to find consistent LLM reasoning paths efficiently
finding: First direct use of Wald SPRT for LLM vote stopping. Tests H0 p=0.5 vs H1 p>0.5 for the top two answers, plus an mSPRT with a Beta prior truncated to (0.5,1]. Argues Adaptive-Consistency ignores Type I error under repeated looks.
numbers: Max 40 samples. AIME24 o3-mini-low: SC@40 70.0%, AC 70.0%, SPRT 80.0%, mSPRT 76.7%; medium 90.0/90.0/90.0/90.0; high 96.7 all. GPQA Diamond o3-mini-low 68.2/67.2/66.7/70.2. GSM gpt-4o-mini 94.2/94.2/93.5/93.9. Token reduction vs SC@40: SPRT 63.9, 84.8, 84.5, 86.2, 88.6 percent; mSPRT 57.3, 76.8, 82.2, 83.6, 88.7; AC 47.9 to 82.8.
limits: p1 shrunk to 0.5001 and Type II error set very high, so Wald's formal guarantees no longer hold. Small benchmark (AIME24 is 30 problems; one problem is 3.3 points). Authors say parameters are hard to set.
agent_relevance: Best published SPRT evidence for LLM vote stopping, but its tuning breaks the guarantee; do not claim error control.

source: ConSol: parameter choices
finding: Textbook SPRT settings (p0,p1 about 0.55-0.6) need more samples than is practical for finding the most frequent of many answers. They shrank p1 to 0.5001 and used a Beta(1e6,1e6) bell prior in the mixture version for sensitivity near 0.5.
numbers: Textbook priors named: Uniform Beta(1,1) and Jeffreys Beta(0.5,0.5). Cap 40 samples; 2-3 samples drawn in parallel per turn to cut wall-clock.
limits: o3-mini and gpt-4o-mini only.
agent_relevance: Close vote shares are where a stop rule cannot be cheap; hard questions simply need more samples.

source: Morandi (2026) Sequential consensus for multi-agent LLM debates: a Wald-SPRT compute governor
finding: SPRT as a stop rule for debate rounds. After each round an LLM judge gives a consensus score in [0,1]; the log likelihood ratio of useful convergence vs not yet useful accumulates until a boundary or a cap Rmax.
numbers: gpt-5, claude-opus-4-6, gemini-2.5-pro; 200 attempted GSM8K and 200 MMLU items; disjoint 40-item calibration sets. GSM8K: 1.01 rounds (4.06 calls) at 97.0% accuracy vs 99.0% for fixed-5 debate (15 calls): 3.7x fewer calls at -2 points. MMLU: hits Rmax=8 on 99.5% of items; accuracy 94.2% matches fixed-5 within noise; judge cannot separate right from wrong consensus (KL near 0).
limits: Guarantees need i.i.d. scores; real scores are autocorrelated (paper simulates the inflation by lag-1 correlation). Judge is an LLM. Negative result on MMLU.
agent_relevance: Caution: a stop rule is only as good as its signal. If the signal cannot separate right from wrong, the rule never fires.

source: Stefan and Schoenbrodt (2023) on peeking, as cited by ConSol
finding: ConSol cites this work for the point that repeated peeking with a fixed-alpha test inflates false positives.
numbers: No figure given in ConSol. Armitage, McPherson, Rowe (1969) numbers not opened.
limits: Secondary citation only; the 2023 paper not read.
agent_relevance: Plain agreement-threshold stops carry hidden error inflation; calibrate on held-out items (G3).

source: Robbins (1970) and Ville (1939), via Howard et al. and Ramdas et al.
finding: Mixture martingales give power-one tests: if the alternative is true the test stops with probability 1; if the null is true the chance the evidence ever reaches 1/alpha is at most alpha (Ville's inequality).
numbers: As stated in the two surveys I read; originals not opened.
limits: Secondary reading.
agent_relevance: A rule we can state: stop when the evidence product passes 1/alpha; error over all looks is at most alpha.

source: Stefan et al. (2022): SPRT in speeded human decisions and classification tests
finding: SPRT has been used to model speeded decisions in humans and animals (Luce 1986; Townsend and Ashby 1983; Bogacz et al. 2006; Ratcliff 1978) and in computerized classification testing (Ferguson 1969; Reckase 1983 with item response theory).
numbers: Pointer only.
limits: Evidence accumulation has its own sibling subfield.
agent_relevance: Same stopping math as drift-diffusion models; link to the Evidence accumulation subfield.

source: Cross-paper pattern: AC, ESC, RASC, DSC
finding: Across AC, ESC, RASC and DSC, savings come mostly from questions where the model already agrees. Weak models and hard sets save little.
numbers: AC: Vicuna-13B 1.9x vs GPT-3.5-Turbo 4.4x. ESC: MATH -33.8% vs GSM8K -80.1%. DSC: CoT equals SC in 84.8% (GPT-3.5) and 96.2% (GPT-4) of GSM8K items.
limits: Different models, datasets and budgets across papers; not a controlled comparison.
agent_relevance: Put the S0 gate first, stop rules second.

source: Stefan et al. (2022): Bayes factor and likelihood ratio
finding: With point priors on all parameters the Bayes factor reduces to a likelihood ratio, so the SPRT is the point-prior limit of the Bayes factor test.
numbers: Informed-prior SBFT is more efficient on average but less robust to misspecification than wide-prior SBFT.
limits: t-test simulations.
agent_relevance: The prior on how often the top answer is right is the main design lever for an agreement stop.

source: Johari et al. (2019): mixture choice and run-length
finding: The mixture that minimises expected run-length matches the prior on effect sizes. Choice of mixture matters, but errors of two orders of magnitude in the variance parameter lose little.
numbers: Within two orders: under 5% average power drop and under 10% run-length increase; run-length stays 20% better for many settings and up to 40% better in some.
limits: Normal-data A/B tests.
agent_relevance: A single wide prior is a safe default when the lead size is unknown.
